Zudilin's Forms at Rational Bases and the Exact Normalised Hankel Order

Erdős #1049 21 pp Equations typeset from the exact TeX
PDFOpen the PDF · 21 pp TeXLaTeX source Source on GitHub Problem dossier

Précis

For coprime integers 𝑎 >𝑏 ≥1,𝐹(𝑎/𝑏) =∑𝑛≥1((𝑎/𝑏)𝑛 −1)−1a>b≥1,F(a/b)=∑n≥1((a/b)n−1)−1 is irrational when log b / log a is less than the explicit cutoff 0.4056830213840605…. This includes every positive integral power of 31/431/4, with irrationality exponent less than 301. The argument uses Zudilin's 2004 forms and constants, cancels common cyclotomic factors before rational evaluation, and computes the remaining denominator cost. For the distinct normalised Hankel determinants VN* in his 2016 construction with x=z=1, the q-order is 𝑁(𝑁 −1)(2𝑁 −1)/6N(N−1)(2N−1)/6 and the leading coefficient is (𝑁!)2(𝑁 +1)!/2𝑁(N!)2(N+1)!/2N. The rational-base criterion does not include 3/23/2; neither argument settles irrationality at that base.

This paper owns the problem-specific exposition for Erdős #1049: the ordinary rational-base irrationality theorem and uniform exponent bound for the (31/4)𝑟(31/4)r family, the exact normalised Hankel order and leading coefficient, the content and endpoint obstructions, and the remaining approximant and remainder construction at 3/23/2.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #1049, which remains open.

Introduction

For 𝑡 >1t>1, expansion of each geometric series gives

𝐹(𝑡)=∑𝑛≥11𝑡𝑛−1=∑𝑛≥1𝜏(𝑛)𝑡𝑛,F(t)=∑n≥11tn−1=∑n≥1τ(n)tn,

where 𝜏(𝑛)τ(n) is the number of positive divisors of 𝑛n. With 𝑞 =1/𝑡q=1/t, this is the 𝑞q-harmonic series ∑𝑛≥1𝑞𝑛/(1 −𝑞𝑛)∑n≥1qn/(1−qn). The rearrangement is justified by nonnegativity, and the resulting series converges since 𝜏(𝑛) ≤𝑛τ(n)≤n and ∑𝑛≥1𝑛𝑡−𝑛 <∞∑n≥1nt−n<∞.

Chowla conjectured that 𝐹(𝑡)F(t) is irrational for every rational 𝑡 >1t>1, as Erdős records ; this is Erdős Problem #1049. The conjecture remains open. We prove a sufficient condition on the numerator and denominator of 𝑡t, using Zudilin’s 2004 construction [4]. The condition includes 31/431/4 and every positive integral power of 31/431/4, but not 3/23/2.

The extra difficulty at a rational base is the denominator. If 𝑈,𝑉 ∈ℤ[𝑋]U,V∈Z[X] have degree at most 𝑊W, then 𝑏𝑊𝑈(𝑎/𝑏)bWU(a/b) and 𝑏𝑊𝑉(𝑎/𝑏)bWV(a/b) are integers. To prove irrationality by these forms, their positive remainders 𝑈(𝑎/𝑏)𝐹(𝑎/𝑏) −𝑉(𝑎/𝑏)U(a/b)F(a/b)−V(a/b) must remain small after multiplication by 𝑏𝑊bW.

A small example shows why cancellation should come first. At 3/23/2, the pair (𝑋 +1)(𝑋 +2),(𝑋 +1)(𝑋 +3)(X+1)(X+2),(X+1)(X+3), cleared with degree bound 22, gives (35,45)(35,45). Cancelling 𝑋 +1X+1 in the polynomial ring and then using degree bound 11 gives (7,9)(7,9). The example is not an approximation to 𝐹F; it illustrates how a common polynomial factor changes the required power of the denominator. For Zudilin’s polynomials the corresponding factors are cyclotomic, and their degrees determine the cutoff below.

For the cancelled polynomials 𝑈𝑛,𝑉𝑛Un,Vn used here, put Λ𝑛 =𝑈𝑛𝐹 −𝑉𝑛Λn=UnF−Vn and 𝑊𝑛 =deg⁡𝑈𝑛Wn=deg⁡Un. We prove deg⁡𝑉𝑛 =𝑊𝑛 −1deg⁡Vn=Wn−1 and

log(𝑏𝑊𝑛Λ𝑛(𝑎/𝑏))=(𝐶1log⁡𝑏−𝐶0log⁡𝑎)𝑛2+𝑜(𝑛2),log(bWnΛn(a/b))=(C1log⁡b−C0log⁡a)n2+o(n2),

where 𝐶0,𝐶1C0,C1 are defined below. If the coefficient of 𝑛2n2 is negative, the forms have integer coefficients and positive values tending to zero. If 𝐹(𝑎/𝑏)F(a/b) were rational, multiplying by its fixed denominator would give positive integers tending to zero, a contradiction.

The proof of the rational-base result occupies Section 2. The independent argument in Section 3 computes the first nonzero term of a Hankel determinant from the 2016 construction. Neither proof uses Section 4, which records supplementary tests for congruence-based arguments at 3/23/2. The companion Zudilin’s Forms at Rational Bases: Proofs and Research Record, called the long record below, gives the additional moment calculations, source comparisons and computational certificates.

Throughout, logarithms are natural. Empty products and determinants have value 11, and a subscripted constant in 𝑂𝑥( ⋅)Ox(⋅) may depend on the fixed base 𝑥x. Other notation is introduced where it is used.

The condition holds for every integer base, since 𝑏 =1b=1 gives log⁡𝑏/log⁡𝑎 =0log⁡b/log⁡a=0. What neither calculation implies.

Theorem 3.2 replaces that band by explicit linear and logarithmic terms and a constant. It changes no cubic coefficient and no prime-power valuation, so it supplies no divisor for the 2004 polynomial forms. Against the two proposed degree savings of long Section 3, the shortfall at 3/23/2 is exactly 𝑁(74𝑁2 −117𝑁 +41)/41 >0N(74N2−117N+41)/41>0 for 𝑁 ≥2N≥2, and the new estimate closes no part of it. Neither assertion supplies the cyclotomic divisibility proved for a different recurrence in [14]. The separate coefficient and content calculations are in long Section 3.3; Appendix A records their sources and finite scope.

The principal proofs are complete. The question here is whether combinations of evaluated rows can be divided by a common integer without losing nonvanishing or smallness of the remainder. This is a different operation from the polynomial cancellation in Section 2. The results below give necessary tests and conditional counting arguments, not such a family.

Primitive integer rows are unimodular modulo every modulus: for (2,3)(2,3) modulo 66, neither coordinate is a unit, but −2 +3 =1−2+3=1. Vanishing minors is an extra assumption. It is imposed in the quotient ring, not in ℤZ: the rows (1,0),(1,6)(1,0),(1,6) below have determinant 66 and coincide modulo 66. Arbitrary primitive rows need not satisfy it; (1,0),(0,1)(1,0),(0,1) have determinant 11. No such approximation family is constructed here.

Lean: pade summand bound and gap.

For the first inequality the gap is zero at 𝑛 =𝑘 =0n=k=0; otherwise both factors are nonnegative. Substituting 𝑗 =𝑛 −𝑚 −1j=n−m−1 gives the second identity for every integer 𝑚m.

Proposition 4.8 (rescaling two integer rows). Multiplying two integer rows by 𝑐1c1 and 𝑐2c2 multiplies their determinant by 𝑐1𝑐2c1c2. The integer identity and its absolute-value form show that the added divisibility is accompanied by exactly the same factor in the real absolute value.

Lean: integer scalar content.

For nonzero row contents 𝑐1,𝑐2c1,c2, write 𝑟𝑖 =𝑐𝑖𝑟prim𝑖ri=ciriprim. Then det(𝑟1,𝑟2) =𝑐1𝑐2det(𝑟prim1,𝑟prim2)det(r1,r2)=c1c2det(r1prim,r2prim) and 𝑟𝑖 ⋅(𝜉, −1) =𝑐𝑖𝑟prim𝑖 ⋅(𝜉, −1)ri⋅(ξ,−1)=ciriprim⋅(ξ,−1). These identities concern multiplication or division of whole integer rows, not cancellation of a polynomial factor before specialisation. Nor does dividing different rows by different contents preserve a fixed residue relation: (1,1) +(5,5)(1,1)+(5,5) is zero modulo 66, but the sum of the primitive rows is (2,2)(2,2). Even contents coprime to the modulus require the residue map to be formed again after row-by-row normalisation.

Residue counts and the index after division

The primitive rows (1,0),(1,6)(1,0),(1,6) generate ℤ ⊕6ℤZ⊕6Z. Modulo 22 this lattice has only two residue vectors, but dividing its even vectors by 22 gives ℤ ⊕3ℤZ⊕3Z, which still has index 33 in ℤ2Z2. Thus a small residue space need not become the full integer lattice after division. Smith normal form gives both quantities in general.

Let a rank-two lattice Λ ⊂ℤ2Λ⊂Z2 be generated by primitive rows, and let 𝑔 >0g>0 be the gcd of their 2 ×22×2 minors. By the description of Smith invariants through gcds of minors , its Smith invariants are 1,𝑔1,g. For 𝐷 ≥1D≥1, therefore

| | |im⁡(Λmod𝐷)| | |=𝐷2gcd(𝑔,𝐷),[ℤ2:Λ∩𝐷ℤ2𝐷]=𝑔gcd(𝑔,𝐷).|im⁡(ΛmodD)|=D2gcd(g,D),[Z2:Λ∩DZ2D]=ggcd(g,D).

A unimodular change of coordinates preserves 𝐷ℤ2DZ2 and reduces both calculations to ℤ ⊕𝑔ℤZ⊕gZ. Thus, when 𝐷 ∣𝑔D∣g, there are only 𝐷D residues, but the divided lattice still has index 𝑔/𝐷g/D. The general formulas without primitive generators are in the long record, Section 10.1.

If two independent divided rows (𝐴𝑖,𝐵𝑖)(Ai,Bi) have |𝐴𝑖| ≤𝐻|Ai|≤H and |𝐴𝑖𝜉 −𝐵𝑖| ≤𝜀|Aiξ−Bi|≤ε, their determinant gives

2𝐻𝜀≥𝑔gcd(𝑔,𝐷).2Hε≥ggcd(g,D).

This is a restriction on two independent forms in the divided lattice. For one nonzero integral form tending to zero, no additional product 𝐻𝜀 →0Hε→0 is required.

A collision must have a small nonzero real remainder

Counting residues within short intervals gives small differences. To keep a difference nonzero, one must also bound the number of selectors with the same residues and the same real value.

Theorem 4.9 (equal residues with close, distinct values). Let 𝐴,𝐵,𝐽A,B,J be finite sets and let 𝑓 :𝐴 →𝐵f:A→B, 𝑔 :𝐴 →ℝg:A→R and 𝜄 :𝐴 →𝐽ι:A→J. Suppose that each simultaneous fibre of (𝑓,𝑔)(f,g) has at most 𝑘k elements and that, for some 𝛿 >0δ>0,

𝜄(𝑥)=𝜄(𝑦)⟹|𝑔(𝑥)−𝑔(𝑦)|<𝛿.ι(x)=ι(y)⟹|g(x)−g(y)|<δ.

If |𝐵||𝐽|𝑘 <|𝐴||B||J|k<|A|, then some distinct 𝑥,𝑦 ∈𝐴x,y∈A satisfy

𝑓(𝑥)=𝑓(𝑦),0<|𝑔(𝑥)−𝑔(𝑦)|<𝛿.f(x)=f(y),0<|g(x)−g(y)|<δ.

Lean: exists small real escape of conditional multiplicity.

Proof. Partition 𝐴A by (𝑓,𝜄)(f,ι). Some cell has more than 𝑘k elements, so its 𝑔g-values cannot all agree. Two unequal values in that cell have the same residue vector and differ by less than 𝛿δ. ◻

Primitivity gives no useful bound on 𝑘k: repeated rows (1,0)(1,0) produce the same sum and remainder for every subset of a given size. The application below therefore needs a separate multiplicity estimate.

Fix positive integers 𝑛,𝐷n,D and 𝑀M primitive integer rows (𝐴𝑗,𝐵𝑗)(Aj,Bj), indexed by 0 ≤𝑗 <𝑀0≤j<M. Put 𝑒𝑗 =𝐴𝑗𝐹(3/2) −𝐵𝑗ej=AjF(3/2)−Bj and apply Theorem 4.9 to binary selectors, with

𝑓(𝜀)=∑𝑗𝜀𝑗(𝐴𝑗,𝐵𝑗)(mod𝐷),𝑔(𝜀)=∑𝑗𝜀𝑗𝑒𝑗.f(ε)=∑jεj(Aj,Bj)(modD),g(ε)=∑jεjej.

For a rank-two lattice generated by these rows, the preceding Smith formula gives 𝑄 ≤𝐷2/gcd(𝑔0,𝐷)Q≤D2/gcd(g0,D), where 𝑔0g0 is the gcd of the minors; it gives no bound on 𝑘k. The selector remainders span an interval of length 𝑇 =∑𝑗|𝑒𝑗|T=∑j|ej|. Subtract its minimum, multiply by 𝑛/𝐷n/D, and take floors. The resulting indices range from 00 to ⌊𝑛𝑇/𝐷⌋⌊nT/D⌋, and two remainders with the same index differ by less than 𝐷/𝑛D/n. Thus a sufficient inequality is

2𝑀>𝑄𝑘(⌊𝑛𝑇𝐷⌋+1).(1)(1)2M>Qk(⌊nTD⌋+1).

It yields a signed row sum divisible coordinatewise by 𝐷D, whose divided real remainder has absolute value strictly between 00 and 1/𝑛1/n. The residue-specific version is in the long record, Section 10.1. The multiplicity bound is what prevents a zero remainder; polynomial nonvanishing does not.

The remaining construction problem

The next question specifies the required integer forms, not an approximation family. Unrestricted, it is equivalent to irrationality of 𝐹(3/2)F(3/2); the long record, Section 10, proves the converse even with the stated index bounds and coefficient height exp⁡(𝑂(𝑛2))exp⁡(O(n2)). A method-specific problem must additionally fix its coefficient formulas, parameter set and permitted normalisations.

Source comparisons and formal verification

Integer-base methods.

Vandehey treats signed coefficients in the digit argument ; Duverney and Tachiya prove linear-independence refinements [11]. Van Assche gives a little 𝑞q-Legendre construction . These integer-base methods are compared in the long record’s related-work section; they are not inputs to the rational specialisation in Section 2.

Coefficient moments.

The coefficient polynomials in [5] give a moment problem different from the remainder moments in Section 3. Long Section 3.3 checks the two leading Hankel families through rank eight, not the all-rank criterion in [15]. For the unshifted family, positivity through rank eight at every real 𝑝 ≥1p≥1 is also a Lean theorem. So is the consequence the long record draws from it: at each rank up to eight, the roots of a determinant polynomial built from Zudilin’s coefficients are real and lie below 𝐹(𝑝)F(p) for every real 𝑝 >1p>1 (finite coefficient positivity and pencil roots). Long Section 3.3 also proves a finite moment representation and discusses (𝑚!)3(m!)3 at the endpoint , formal continued fractions and finite quadrature [17][18]. It also gives complete polynomial contents through rank five and specified cyclotomic residue tests through rank eight. These finite results do not assert all-rank coefficient positivity or divisibility.

Functional equations.

Bell and Smertnig’s classification [9] excludes 𝑘k-Mahler equations for 𝐿(𝑧) =∑𝑛≥1𝜏(𝑛)𝑧𝑛L(z)=∑n≥1τ(n)zn when 𝑘 ≥2k≥2: there is no polynomial-coefficient relation among 𝐿(𝑧),𝐿(𝑧𝑘),…,𝐿(𝑧𝑘𝑑)L(z),L(zk),…,L(zkd) with a nonzero coefficient of 𝐿(𝑧)L(z). The single-base exclusion is also a Lean theorem, in the form that for every 𝑘 ≥2k≥2 no finite-dimensional ℚ(𝑧)Q(z)-subspace of ℚ((𝑧))Q((z)) containing 𝐿L is stable under 𝑧 ↦𝑧𝑘z↦zk (single-base statement). Long Section 10.3 explains this functional obstruction; it gives no irrationality statement for 𝐿(2/3) =𝐹(3/2)L(2/3)=F(3/2).

Formal sources and finite computations.

In the supplied snapshot, PaperR17/SourceConsumers.lean constructs the cancelled forms and proves the irrationality and measure results; AllRow/Producer.lean constructs the transformed rows and proves the all-rank determinant formulas.

The index distinguishes reported public, parallel-release and unbuilt material; no new Lean run is claimed for the indexed material. The linked invertible-coordinate theorem is weaker than the ordinary unimodular-row theorem. Apart from the rank-eight positivity of the unshifted family, the finite computations described above are not Lean proofs; their certificates and reproduction scripts are in the long record. Historical links retain their original revisions and line numbers, which have not been revalidated. Long Appendix A records the snapshot identifiers and gives the full source guide.

six conditions for clearing a window; necessary power-versus-linear inequality; 3𝑥 <2𝑥+13x<2x+1 for 𝑥 ≥2x≥2; rational-base partial sum; one-term extension of the partial sum; scaled remainder; subtracted term in the recurrence; exponential lower bound for that term; integer-base special case; rational comparison for 7/27/2.
